props.title: Nouvelle Vague

sections.content: Nouvelle Vague represents Jean-Luc Godard's meta-commentary on the very movement he helped create. The film layers references to classic Hollywood cinema while featuring Alain Delon in a dual role that deliberately recalls his earlier New Wave performances in Purple Noon (1960) and Le Samouraï (1967). Godard's late-period experimentation reaches a fascinating peak here, fragmenting narrative conventions while exploring themes of capitalism, rebirth, and the death of classical cinema.

sections.content: The French New Wave revolutionized cinema between 1959-1968. The 400 Blows (1959) launched the movement with its fresh take on youth and rebellion, while Hiroshima Mon Amour (1959) brought radical new approaches to time and memory. The Cahiers du Cinéma critics-turned-filmmakers like François Truffaut, Claude Chabrol, and Godard rejected traditional "quality" cinema in favor of personal expression and formal experimentation.

By 1990, Godard had moved far beyond his early style into increasingly abstract territory. Nouvelle Vague serves as both celebration and eulogy for the movement, incorporating dense literary references and philosophical dialogue. The film's complex sound design layers multiple languages and voices, creating what Godard called "music of ideas." It connects to his later works like Film Socialisme (2010) and Goodbye to Language (2014) in its radical deconstruction of conventional cinema. SUBHEAD: Late Godard and Contemporary Cinema

sections.content: Nouvelle Vague anticipates many concerns of contemporary art cinema. Its fragmented narrative and emphasis on texture over plot influenced directors like Claire Denis in High Life (2018) and Leos Carax in Holy Motors (2012). The film's critique of capitalism and media resonates with later works like David Cronenberg's Cosmopolis (2012) and Oliver Assayas's Personal Shopper (2016).
